speaker: Doctor
text:
I have noted your history of gait and limb ataxia. I will need to ask you a few specific questions about your symptoms and perform an examination to determine the exact cause.

Let's begin: How long have you been experiencing these balance and coordination issues?

speaker: Patient
text: I started having trouble walking recently, and people say I look drunk when I walk. I also feel clumsy in my arms and legs, especially on the right side.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that information. The "drunk" gait and clumsiness suggest significant cerebellar involvement. You mentioned the right side is worse; is this ataxia new, or has it been worsening progressively over time?

speaker: Patient
text: I have Crohn disease and it has been difficult to control. I have been taking natalizumab for about a year.

speaker: Doctor
text: The combination of new-onset, progressive ataxia and your history of Crohn's disease raises immediate concern for an adverse reaction to natalizumab. Given the timeline, I need to know if you have experienced any recent changes in vision, such as double vision or a loss of vision in one eye, which would suggest Immune Effector Cell-associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome (ICANS) or an acute relapse. REQUEST TEST: MRI Brain with contrast.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: MRI_Brain Findings: Lesions consistent with Progressive Multifocal Encephalopathy (PML). Comments: T1/T2 images showing multifocal demyelinating lesions without gadolinium enhancement, indicative of PML.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) secondary to natalizumab therapy.

The MRI findings of non-enhancing multifocal demyelinating lesions in the context of your recent ataxia confirm PML. We must immediately discontinue natalizumab and consider starting a disease-modifying treatment for Crohn's disease to reduce the risk of recurrence.
